Side by side, and how they were received
The letters beside the Gospel and beside each other, and how the church received them.
BESIDE THE GOSPEL
1 John and the Gospel of John
1 John beside the Gospel of John. Click a ribbon to keep it.

Twenty-six places where 1 John and John's Gospel share wording or ideas, each named by Westcott, Law, Brooke or Dionysius of Alexandria. Dionysius already observed in the third century that “the Gospel and Epistle agree with each other and begin in the same manner”; Westcott calls the two openings complementary rather than parallel. Pairs marked “wording” share a phrase or a rare word; the rest share an idea. 1 John 1:1–4 John 1:1–18 [13][1][5][2]
ECHOES
2 John's echoes of 1 John
2 John beside 1 John. Click a ribbon to keep it.
2 John repeats 1 John's teaching almost line for line. Law calls it in effect a summary of the first letter.[5][9]
TWIN NOTES
2 John and 3 John
2 John beside 3 John. Click a ribbon to keep it.

The two short letters open and close in the same words. Brooke sets them side by side and says the likeness points to one author writing at about the same time. They are almost exactly the same length, which Brooke thinks was probably set by the size of an ordinary papyrus sheet.[2][5]

How they were received
